title: Nanopillar metasurfaces uniting high optical reflectivity with ultracoherent nanomechanics
authors: Alexander Jung, Anastasiia Ciers, Hannes Pfeifer, Albert Hansson, Johanna Örgård, Daniel Stachanow, Viktor A. Lilja, Philippe Tassin, Witlef Wieczorek
abstract: Mechanically compliant mirrors are key components in cavity optomechanics. However, the requirements to achieve the best optical and mechanical performance are usually in direct competition. A high reflectivity for tightly focused beams entails thick reflectors, whereas ultracoherent flexural nanomechanics necessitates thin membranes. We eliminate this trade-off by introducing high-refractive-index nanopillar metasurfaces on top of a thin membrane. We pattern a 50 micrometer-diameter array of nanopillars to form a photonic crystal. The flat band behavior of guided resonances in the photonic crystal enables a reflectivity of 99.82(1)% for a tightly focused beam of 7 micrometer waist. The combination of two guided resonances creates a 100 nanometer-wide high-reflectivity band around 1550 nanometer. Simultaneously, the nanopillar patterning realizes a density-modulated phononic crystal that isolates an ultracoherent localized mechanical mode with a $Q\cdot f$-product of $2\cdot 10^{14}$Hz. The demonstrated nanopillar metasurfaces enable lightweight mirrors for room-temperature quantum optomechanics and for use as levitated mirrors or lightsails.
summary: This paper presents a breakthrough in optomechanics by developing nanopillar metasurfaces that overcome the conflict between high optical reflectivity and thin mechanical membranes. By engineering the structure as a photonic crystal, they achieve near-perfect reflectivity while simultaneously creating an ultra-coherent mechanical resonator, enabling lightweight, room-temperature quantum optomechanical devices.
main_problem: The primary challenge is overcoming the inherent trade-off in optomechanics where high optical reflectivity requires thick structures, while achieving ultracoherent nanomechanics demands thin membranes.
main_result: The authors successfully designed and demonstrated nanopillar metasurfaces that simultaneously achieve high optical reflectivity ($\sim 99.82\%$) and support an ultracoherent mechanical mode ($Q\cdot f$-product of $2\cdot 10^{14}	ext{Hz}$) at room temperature.
method: The methodology involves patterning high-refractive-index nanopillars to form a photonic crystal (PhC) on a thin membrane, which is characterized using both optical (reflectivity/cavity) and mechanical (NPS/ring-down) measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is a high-refractive-index nanopillar metasurface patterned on a thin membrane, forming both a photonic crystal (for light) and a density-modulated phononic crystal (for mechanics). The performance is analyzed using QNM theory for optics and standard mechanical resonance characterization for mechanics.
key_observables: Optical reflectivity ($R \approx 99.82\%$), mechanical quality factor ($Q \cdot f$-product $\approx 2\cdot 10^{14}	ext{Hz}$), and the single-photon cooperativity ($C_q$).
important_parameters: Membrane thickness ($35	ext{ nm}$), nanopillar array period ($a_{	ext{PhC}} = 0.74\ \mu	ext{m}$), and room temperature ($300	ext{ K}$) operation.
main_assumptions: The quantum control analysis relies on 'optimistic parameters' for future experiments, and the optical loss is attributed to material absorption in the a-Si nanopillars.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the nPhC structure, the interaction of Gaussian beams, band diagrams showing guided resonances, SEM images of fabricated devices, and measurements of reflectivity spectra and mechanical noise power spectra.
paper_structure: The paper addresses the fundamental trade-off, introduces the nanopillar metasurface solution, details the optical characterization (reflectivity measurements), and then integrates this with mechanical characterization to demonstrate room-temperature quantum optomechanical functionality.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of integrating high-performance optical cavities with high-quality mechanical resonators, which is a cornerstone problem in quantum optomechanics and cavity QED.
